items.title: RT Amrish Rau: Today, Parliament moved an amendment to the Payment & Settlement Act, which is a step in the right direction towards implementing MDR i...
items.description_html:
RT Amrish Rau
Today, Parliament moved an amendment to the Payment & Settlement Act, which is a step in the right direction towards implementing MDR in some shape or form—without impacting customers, while allowing the recovery of reasonable charges from merchants for higher-value transactions that already attract such charges on debit and credit cards.

While this will undoubtedly bring about a debate, it is important to remember that both Brazil’s PIX and China’s real-time payment systems have always had merchant charges of 30-40bps. Yet both have achieved over 90% penetration across users and merchants, compared to roughly 35–40% in India, as per reports published by the RBI and NPCI.

UPI today processes nearly 23 billion interoperable payment transactions every month—the largest real-time payment system in the world. Looking at the near-zero investment scenario over the last six years, the pace of growth is naturally slowing, even though there is still an opportunity to increase penetration by almost 3x across both consumers and merchants.

For us to get to 90% penetration, and to take UPI global, startups, fintechs, and banks will need to fund this expansion through continued investments in IT, innovation, and cyber security. These costs have increased by almost 300% over the last 12–24 months. While there should be some recovery of these investments, P2P transactions—and charges to consumers—should continue to remain zero.

There has always been a monetisation model for electricity, water, roads, and mobile phones, even when much of the infrastructure has been built by the government. That is what has enabled these sectors to keep investing, expand access, and fuel economic growth.

Achieving 90% penetration will drive significant formalisation of the economy, reduce the use of cash, enable flow-based credit for small businesses—which is the need of the hour—and create immense long-term benefits for the country.

Something important to Adress:

A lot of you keep asking and sending me queries on why I do not charge or have a product for retail clients in the market as many of you have expressed tremendous interest to be clients , and till date I have charged absolutely Zero Rupees from anyone on this platform as a matter of principle and not taken any charges

At Value Equity , we are currently consulting few family offices , research desks , UHNI's and more on India research that is loaded with differentiated insights on many Indian companies , and that has been the core of this for the last few years and takes up most of my time and effort catering to larger clients and houses

But now , a lot of you on high demand have asked me to create something for the wider audience that can help you all capture these insights too, and hence I am deciding to start something on this front soon , to make institutional grade , differentiated insights filled access to you all who have been here and supported my work

We intend to keep it limited as bandwidth to provide such high quality research is time consuming , but I have started work on this..

If you folks are interested and would like to be in the loop on this , do comment your interest as I intend to keep it limited

items.title: Had this happened on expiry day, the market would have been staring at a full-blown disaster ! A few thoughts, 1. On expiry days - even when cash pric...
items.description_html:
Had this happened on expiry day, the market would have been staring at a full-blown disaster !

A few thoughts,

1. On expiry days - even when cash prices shut at 3.15 PM - option premiums will continue to be high because - when anything can happen in the next moment who will want to square off ? So the natural time collapse of the premium won't happen !

2. Wouldn't mutual fund NAVs go haywire ? If someone had given sale notice today - he/she get today's high but 'wrong prices'. And tomorrow pre-open should gap-down ?

3. If there was a index rebalance today - wouldn't the fund have rebalanced at the 'wrong price' ?

Problem seems to be that markets did not have the required depth. The system & tech may have worked as they were supposed to - but did we get better & more accurate prices ? The answer is an obvious & clear No !

The idea was to reduce tracking error for index itself - the problem is the index itself became a tracking error.

I know it was only Day 1 & things should get better as everyone gets the hang of it - but still - it would not be a bad idea for everyone to look at the unintended consequences of this.

items.title: Syngene failed to deliver 23% ROCE. Praj did in 2022. Syngene failed to deliver 31% ROCE. Praj did in 2023. Syngene failed to deliver 29% ROCE. Praj d...
items.description_html:
Syngene failed to deliver 23% ROCE. Praj did in 2022.

Syngene failed to deliver 31% ROCE. Praj did in 2023.

Syngene failed to deliver 29% ROCE. Praj did in 2024.

If Praj is the benchmark for the sector, then the obvious question is: who is the other Praj inside and outside India?

Syngene is not the sector. There are at least 6 players that have been materially superior to Syngene on both ROCE and growth in India. More importantly, they have demonstrated high ROCE alongside strong PAT growth and CAGR over long periods. Syngene has not.

I think that is a fair standard. A consistent yardstick to rate them. Syngene deserves the opportunity to prove its worth, but it also deserves to be judged on its record. They have been around for over 30 years now. Manufacturing talk was loud and clear even in 2015 (IPO TAWK). That is enough time to assess what the operating system has actually produced.

Several CDMOs started years after Syngene and have already raced ahead. And they are unlikely to stand still while Syngene catches up.

The burden of proof is now on Syngene, not on the sector.


Vibhor Vaish: @unseenvalue @unseenvalue Sir, any such views on Praj Industries. Do you see their talk as TAWK as well ? I believe they have had sufficient time at their hands as well. What keeps Praj Multi cylinder as an irondome while syngene' taj as a hollow palace.

What happens next needs to be decided. I also announced last night that an understanding on the safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz is a necessary condition for the opening of Hormuz, but it is not a sufficient condition. The Strait of Hormuz is not closed because of a disagreement between Iran and Oman; Hormuz has been in trouble since March of last year due to the military aggression of the United States and the Zionist regime..."

"As long as America's evil continues, as long as the naval blockade of Iran is declared, as long as America's military aggression against Iran and its interests continues, and as long as all the things that America has violated during this period continue, there will be no significant change in the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, the focus of the negotiations with Oman will be on this issue, and the issues related to Iran and the United States should be examined in the next stages to see in which direction the situation will go..."

items.description_html:
Urban Company Q1FY27 - Strong Core Business

Cons. NTV increased 42% YoY to 1,465 Cr, while REV grew 44% to 528 Cr

Total orders increased 79% YoY to 13.2 Mn. Company added 1.2 Mn new customers during the quarter, taking annual transacting users to 9.3 Mn

India Consumer Services

India Consumer Services NTV increased 29% YoY to 1,056 Cr, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of growth acceleration

Growth has accelerated for 4 straight quarters:
10% → 19% → 21% → 26% → 29%

Adj EBITDA margin improved to 6.9% of NTV from 5.2% YoY, moving closer to the long term guidance of 9-10%

International NTV increased 76% YoY to 237 Cr

Management does not plan to enter new countries in the near term and will focus on scaling India, UAE, Singapore & Saudi Arabia

Native NTV increased 51% YoY to 119 Cr, while net REV grew 60% to 95 Cr

Adj EBITDA loss narrowed to 7.3% of NTV from 11.4% YoY, with management indicating visibility of profitability over the next few quarters

Native will remain focused on premium water purifiers & smart locks, with only limited expansion into additional categories

Insta Help delivered 3.82 Mn orders, up 43% QoQ

Adj EBITDA loss stood at 132 Cr, although loss per order improved to 346 from 447 in Q4FY26 due to better micro market density

Management estimates an addressable market of 7,000-12,000 Cr across the top 15 cities & remains focused on gaining market leadership

However, management expects Insta Help to remain a structurally low margin business, with eventual margins likely in the low single digits

The business is not expected to generate meaningful profits over the next five years, with break even targeted by FY31

Cons adj EBITDA loss stood at 65 Cr, entirely driven by Insta Help

Excluding Insta Help, the remaining businesses generated adjusted EBITDA of 67 Cr, more than doubling YoY

Company holds cash of 2,019 Cr, broadly unchanged sequentially despite the aggressive investment in Insta Help

Management retained guidance of cons. adj EBITDA break even by Q3FY28 & adj EBITDA of 1,000 Cr by FY31

HAL, keep an eye out -

You know the main concern with HAL, it’s not their order book, which is huge. The main concern was order execution. GE is likely to start delivering two jet engines for the Tejas programme in August and another 20 engines by the end of the year.

That should solve the order backlog issue because the aircraft manufacturing bottleneck is solved by HAL

The problem was that GE had stopped manufacturing the GE 404 engine, and they had to restart the manufacturing along with reactivating the entire supply chain, which is now fully active. The Indian GE engine variant is called GE F404-IN20

There are no other ‘manufacturing’ bottlenecks. GE has set up a dedicated line for the Indian variant. HAL has 15 aircraft ready without engines and 6 with engines.

24 units capacity in Bangalore and another 12 units in Nashik - So that makes 36 aircrafts

Swish wants to close that gap through its own consumer interface and a 10-minute delivery promise.

items.title: India has seen a big push towards financial inclusion over the last two decades. Having a bank account is an important first step in that journey, all...
items.description_html:
India has seen a big push towards financial inclusion over the last two decades. Having a bank account is an important first step in that journey, allowing account-holders to receive welfare benefits, save, borrow and invest.

From fewer than half of Indian households having a bank account in 2006, 96% of households had a bank account by 2021, according to the National Family Health Survey. However, this doesn’t mean that men and women are accessing banking at equal rates.

Of the 2.6 billion bank accounts now held by individuals in India, men hold 50% more bank accounts than women. These numbers can include multiple accounts held by the same person, but exclude institutional accounts held by corporations or trusts.

Gender inequalities are also evident in how Indian men and women use their bank accounts. According to the World Bank's Global Findex Database 2025, one in five bank accounts held by women are inactive, compared to just over one in ten among men.

items.description_html:
BREAKING: Global household net worth surged +7.3% YoY, to a record $570 trillion in 2025.

This was primarily driven by equities which accounted for 57% of the increase, while real estate contributed just 15%.

Since 2000, this figure has risen +338%, with an average annual increase of +5.9%.

As a result, global household net worth is now equivalent to ~380% of world GDP.

Real estate accounts for ~50% of the total, followed by equities and investment funds at ~25%, bonds and pensions at 20%, and cash deposits at 20%.

This is somewhat offset by loans, which equal ~15% of the full amount.

Among countries, US household net worth stood at $175 trillion last year, +133% above China's $75 trillion and +661% above Germany's $23 trillion.

Own assets or be left behind.

Foreign investors are piling back into South Korean equities:

Investors outside of South Korea purchased +$5.4 billion of South Korean stocks on Friday, the largest daily purchase on record.

Meanwhile, domestic retail investors sold a record -$5.5 billion of equities, marking their 3rd consecutive daily sale.

This marks a sharp reversal after foreign investors sold -$110 billion of Korean stocks in 2026 prior to Friday's session.

Over the same period, domestic retail investors purchased +$67 billion, including +$57 billion in May and June alone.

Furthermore, deposits held at Korean retail brokerages for stock purchases dropped -$23 billion from their June peak, to ~$74 billion.

Foreign capital appears to be returning to South Korea.

Warsh essentially questioned whether PCE should remain the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge.

He initially called PCE the “proper standard” measure. But then came the curveball - "who knows what the Fed might say about its strategy after next January, especially once the task forces have had their say"

The concern is that he could move the inflation goalposts by changing the measure the Fed targets. And that these task forces may simply be there to rubber-stamp the chair’s preferred policy.

items.title: India’s app-store market has crossed a $1 billion revenue run rate. In-app purchases on Google Play and Apple’s App Store reached a record $345 mill...
items.description_html:
India’s app-store market has crossed a $1 billion revenue run rate.

In-app purchases on Google Play and Apple’s App Store reached a record $345 million in Q2 2026, according to Sensor Tower.

That is nearly $1.4 billion annualised.

But even at that level, India accounts for less than 1% of global app-store revenue.

For years, global app-store spending was dominated by mobile games. India has never been a major spender on gaming.

That balance is only now shifting globally as non-gaming apps overtook games for the first time in 2025, but still accounted for only slightly more than half of spending.

India presents a more extreme contrast:

- Non-gaming apps now generate about 70% of India’s app-store revenue vs 50-51% globally.

- Non-gaming revenue grew more than 50% YoY to nearly $240 million in Q2 2026, compared with 10% growth in gaming revenue to $106 million.

Entertainment/video apps such as YouTube, Instagram, Crunchyroll and JioHotstar, as well as AI, productivity and utility apps such as Google One, ChatGPT, Claude and LinkedIn, dominate the Indian market in revenues.

Interestingly, Claude’s revenue surged more than 19-fold YoY in Q2, according to Sensor Tower.

items.title: There are two reasons saving is so high, Gita. One, as you noted, is precautionary saving. With the economy slowing and employment uncertainty rising,...
items.description_html:
There are two reasons saving is so high, Gita. One, as you noted, is precautionary saving. With the economy slowing and employment uncertainty rising, that is hardly surprising. The standard IMF and World Bank recommendation is to strengthen the social safety net., but even if Beijing were to introduce Scandinavian-style welfare provisions tomorrow, the credibility of the system is so low that it would take many years, perhaps even decades, before household saving behavior changed materially. We saw this last year with the pension reforms. Very few workers chose to contribute to the new system because, they argued, they were unlikely ever to receive the promised benefits.

The more important reason for China's exceptionally high saving, however, is simply the extraordinarily low household share of GDP. Households must receive, directly or indirectly, a much larger share of what they produce. There are essentially two ways to accomplish this, but each comes with its own costs.

The sustainable solution is to redistribute income from businesses and governments to households. This can be done in many ways: raising wages, appreciating the currency, increasing deposit rates, eliminating the hukou system, strengthening labor protections, and so on. But none of these change can possible happen quickly enough to matter to China's trade partners, and, as you point out, none of these policies is painless. They would almost certainly slow growth by reducing the profitability of manufacturers that are already struggling to earn returns.

The alternative, and the one you seem to prefer, is to increase fiscal transfers to households without reducing the fiscal support that currently subsidizes investment in manufacturing and infrastructure.

That might have been a reasonable proposal fifteen years ago, or perhaps even ten, but China already has one of the highest debt burdens in the world relative to GDP (second only to Japan's) and by far the fastest-growing. To argue that China should postpone a difficult but necessary adjustment by allowing debt to grow even faster strikes me as a poor recommendation in light of the historical evidence.

The fundamental point is that China's low consumption share is not a temporary weakness but a structural feature of its growth model, and one that has been central to the explosive expansion of its share of global manufacturing. It took Japan eighteen years, from 1991 to 2008, to raise its consumption share of GDP by just ten percentage points, even though Japan began with smaller domestic imbalances and far lower debt levels than China has today. Even if China achieved the same adjustment, its consumption share of GDP would still remain exceptionally low.

During those eighteen years, however, Japan's GDP growth averaged well below 1%. What is less widely remembered is that Japan's share of global manufacturing fell by more than half over the same period. That was no coincidence. Then, as now in China, manufacturing competitiveness depended in large part on the systematic transfer of resources, directly and indirectly, from households to producers and investment.

It seems to me that you want to propose a way for China to enjoy the benefits of a profound structural transformation in its economy without bearing any of the associated costs, by relying on an even faster increase in an already alarming debt burden. This, among other cases, is essentially what Brazil and the Soviet Union attempted in the 1970s, and Japan in the 1980s. In every case, postponing the adjustment only ensured that it became much more difficult later.

My final point is a practical one. There are many precedents for the European Union demanding that large external imbalances be addressed through exchange-rate adjustment. There are almost none for demanding that a trading partner eliminate the hukou system, transform its social welfare system, raise wages, strengthen labor unions, liberalize interest rates, or undertake any number of other politically difficult domestic reforms quickly enough to matter for Europe's economy.

I do not think anyone, including Brad Setser, is arguing that currency appreciation is the only way to resolve China's domestic imbalances, or even necessarily the best way. It may, however, be one of the very few adjustment mechanisms that China's trading partners can realistically expect Beijing to implement within a timeframe that matters to them.

items.title: BREAKING: The US personal savings rate fell -0.1 percentage point in June, to 2.7%, the lowest since June 2022. This marks the 5th consecutive monthly...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: The US personal savings rate fell -0.1 percentage point in June, to 2.7%, the lowest since June 2022.

This marks the 5th consecutive monthly decline, bringing the cumulative drop to -1.7 percentage points.

This is also the 3rd-lowest monthly reading since April 2008, during the Financial Crisis.

To put this into perspective, the personal savings rate averaged ~5.5% between 2014 and 2019.

The only period in modern history with similarly low saving rates was 2005-2007, when the rate fluctuated between 1.4% and 3.3%.

US households are struggling to save money.

items.title: China’s economy is losing momentum: China's manufacturing PMI fell -1.1 points in July, to 49.2, one of the lowest readings since 2023. This also mar...
items.description_html:
China’s economy is losing momentum:

China's manufacturing PMI fell -1.1 points in July, to 49.2, one of the lowest readings since 2023.

This also marks the first reading below 50 since February, signaling contraction in the sector.

At the same time, non-manufacturing PMI, measuring construction and services activity, declined -1.2 points, to 49.0, the lowest since December 2022.

Construction PMI alone dropped 2.0 points, to 47.0 points, the lowest since the 2020 pandemic.

On top of this, China’s GDP growth slowed to just +4.3% YoY in Q2 2026, the weakest expansion since Q4 2022.

China’s slowdown is spreading across its economy.

This figure has more than tripled since the start of 2024.

As a result, more ETFs have launched over the last 2 months than during the entire first half of 2024.

Of all ETFs introduced this year, 54% incorporate derivatives, and over 33% are classified as leveraged or inverse funds.

Furthermore, fund issuers have already filed for more than 1,000 leveraged ETFs so far this year, pointing to another wave of launches ahead.

The ETF market is expanding faster than ever.

items.title: Asia's leverage boom is rapidly reversing: Margin debt in South Korea has declined -$4 billion from its June peak, to $22 billion, the lowest since mi...
items.description_html:
Asia's leverage boom is rapidly reversing:

Margin debt in South Korea has declined -$4 billion from its June peak, to $22 billion, the lowest since mid-April.

At the same time, stock margin loans in China have dropped -$59 billion, to $385 billion, the lowest since the 2nd week of April.

Similarly, in Taiwan, margin debt has fallen -$4 billion from its July peak, to $15 billion, the lowest since mid-May.

Combined, margin debt across these three markets has declined by a massive -$67 billion.

On top of that, South Korea-listed leveraged ETFs linked to SK Hynix and Samsung have lost -$7 billion in assets since their June peak, down -63%, to $4 billion.

Leverage is amplifying historic volatility across Asian markets.

Although the government later declared the crisis over, families continue to pay higher prices, while those without registered LPG connections often have little choice but to rely on the black market.

But what if India already has an alternative?

In this documentary, @down2earthindia travels from urban neighbourhoods affected by rising LPG costs to villages in western Uttar Pradesh, where dung cakes have long been used as a cooking fuel. But dung cakes are not a clean fuel, and they cannot be used in cities.

So, the question becomes: can India take this same raw material and convert it into a clean fuel that can reach the whole country?

items.title: I have been tracking the semiconductor sector for a while now ASML getting caught in geopolitics prompted it to partner with Indian Fabs A geopolitica...
items.description_html:
I have been tracking the semiconductor sector for a while now

ASML getting caught in geopolitics prompted it to partner with Indian Fabs

A geopolitically neutral manufacturing and engineering base makes strategic sense. But I don't think it stops there.

ASML will meaningfully expand in India with the localization of at least some components, especially as India pushes deeper domestic value addition under its semiconductor policies.

ISM 2.0 also seems likely to move beyond just attracting fabs. The Government is said to plan to back promising semiconductor startups through equity stakes and the ecosystem could become much more integrated (as it goes just beyond fabs)

Reports of Tata discussing sub-assembly production and component manufacturing for ASML's EUV ecosystem are incredibly exciting. Just imagine this.

An EUV machine costs well north of $400 million.

Even if Indian companies eventually contribute just 5% of the bill of materials, the revenue opportunity may not be transformational on day one—but the perception shift would be enormous.

Supplying components to the world's most advanced manufacturing machine would put Indian engineering on a completely different map.

The semiconductor story isn't just about making chips. It's about everything else as well!

It's about becoming indispensable to the global supply chain

Exciting times for India indeed! Dil thaam ke baithiye :)

items.title: SCMP: "After blanketing the country in railways, expressways, airports and seagoing canals to reach a 91 per cent completion rate, the push for the ne...
items.description_html:
SCMP: "After blanketing the country in railways, expressways, airports and seagoing canals to reach a 91 per cent completion rate, the push for the next 4 percentage points raises questions for the world’s second-largest economy: what’s left to build, and how are massive projects being justified when the nation’s most economically vibrant regions are already connected?"

The answer, of course, is that the rush to expand the country's transportation system has much less to do with the economic benefits of an expanded transportation system and much more to do with the need to shift investment out of China's already-excessive investment in manufacturing, which was itself the result of the need to shift investment out of China's excessive investment in property.

Since the contraction in China's trade surplus after the GFC, Beijing's consistent strategy has been to shift investment into another sector whenever excess capacity and debt has made the previous sector unsustainable.

But with property investment, infrastructure investment, and manufacturing investment already excessive, and the country's debt burden rising so quickly, it takes more and more imagination to find a new area of investment that can be justified.

items.title: There are two ways to find margin in quick commerce, and they're worth very different multiples. One is to pull discounts and raise fees. Quick to sho...
items.description_html:
There are two ways to find margin in quick commerce, and they're worth very different multiples.

One is to pull discounts and raise fees. Quick to show up, and it unwinds the moment someone undercuts you. The other is to build revenue that doesn't trade against volume.

Instamart's June quarter looks like the second. Revenue per order rose from Rs 97 to Rs 108, and adjusted revenue grew 43% against 40% GOV growth — monetisation running ahead of the business, on brand take rates, advertising and platform fees.

The cross-check is the basket. Net AOV is Rs 508 against Blinkit's Rs 518. Two years ago that gap was Rs 111. Closing it to Rs 7 while taking more per order isn't a pricing trick. The assortment changed.

- Negative working capital
- Higher average order value
- Lower cash burn

For context, Zepto’s reported AOV is Rs 330-370, compared with Rs 518 for market leader Blinkit and Rs 511 for Swiggy Instamart.

So Zepto would need to increase the AOV by 40-50% to catch up.

items.title: RT The Khel India: MEET 23-YEAR-OLD ASMITA DEY 🇮🇳🥹 Born in a small village in Tripura, Asmita is the daughter of a bicycle mechanic who strug...
items.description_html:
RT The Khel India
MEET 23-YEAR-OLD ASMITA DEY 🇮🇳🥹

Born in a small village in Tripura, Asmita is the daughter of a bicycle mechanic who struggled every day to provide for his family.

They were so poor that they depended on ration cards just to put food on the table.

When 12-year-old Asmita left home after being selected in a talent search, her father folded his hands before her coach and made just one request:

“Sir, we’re very small people. Please help my daughter become someone.”

That one sentence became her life’s purpose.

She spent years away from home, travelling for days to compete, often without confirmed train tickets, chasing a dream that seemed impossible.

Then, heartbreak struck ❤️‍🩹

Just days before qualifying for the Commonwealth Games, her father passed away after suffering a brain stroke.

She flew home, performed his last rites, and quietly returned to training.

Today, with tears in her eyes, Asmita Dey fulfilled her late father’s dream by becoming India’s first-ever Commonwealth Games Judo Gold Medallist. 🥇🇮🇳

He couldn’t be there to watch her stand on top of the podium.

But every step she took was for him.

Some victories are far bigger than medals.

This is one of them. 🫡🥹

Heartbroken & so inspired 💔💔🙏🏽

The Commonwealth Games is becoming a daily roll-call of young Indians who have emerged from unimaginable hardship & horrors to win gold.

Look at 23-year-old judoka Asmita Dey, who is now the first Indian to win Commonwealth Games gold in the women’s 48kg category.

7 months ago, she lost her father to a brain stroke. A bicycle mechanic who earned barely ₹300 a day, he raised his family in a mud house in a small village in Tripura. When a knee injury threatened Asmita’s career, he found the money to take her to Delhi for treatment.

Even as the family mourned, Asmita’s mother urged her daughter to return to training, believing that abandoning the dream would betray everything her father had sacrificed for.

I have a few multibagger stocks in my portfolio

The journey of holding them made me a better person in life

The journey of a multibagger is anything but smooth - quarterly misses, many unseen factors affecting the business/ your holdings, stock corrections, patience gets tested, and folks usually write off the stocks or have negative views

Holding multibaggers teaches you Investing and Life in a better way

It tells you that direction is more important than speed, patience, tells you that life is full of speedbreakers and that you may reach your destination a bit late, but you will definitely reach it, and that ups and downs are part of both investing and Life. Also, just keeping your head down and keeping that conviction is so important, even though the Whole world may be against you or that stock

Thank you, Financial Markets and Investing, for making me a better person

I came here to make money, but I got so much more. I got multibagger people in life who held my hand and took me ahead in my life, career, and markets

Warren Buffett says just 5 stocks can change your life, and I agree

items.title: RT Ajay Rotti: At the outset, I state that the data used and extracted here are correct. I cannot disagree with that. However, I cannot get myself to ...
items.description_html:
RT Ajay Rotti
At the outset, I state that the data used and extracted here are correct. I cannot disagree with that. However, I cannot get myself to agree with the conclusion or the headline. The conclusion reached requires much stronger evidence not just income tax return data at 30,000 feet level. Why? Here are some reasons:

1. The first issue is treatment of personal income tax data as a proxy for entrepreneurial income is incorrect. India has a large number of closely held businesses structured as small private limited companies, partnerships and LLPs. The way the entrepreneur's returns look is very different.

Profits are taxed at the entity level, and partners often receive exempt profit shares rather than taxable business income. They may deploy those exempt profits into interest/dividend yielding assets and offer only those to tax.

My own case: I run a Private limited company. My return will look like a small salary with higher interest/capital gains income. My return looks like a "Rentier" returns. But my activity is anything but rentier. My returns earlier as a Partner of a professional services firm looked worse. Largely exempt professional income and only "rentier" income.

2. The second issue is the characterization of dividend income as "rentier" or passive income. Dividends received by promoters are fundamentally different from dividends earned by a passive investor holding a diversified stock portfolio. Dividends earned by Shiv Nadar or Azim Premji cannot be called "Rentier" income. And these are big enough to skew the statistics.

3. A third point is that the article appears to equate the "head of income" (a legal concept in income-tax) with its economic substance. Business owners have considerable flexibility in how they extract returns ie salary, dividends, interest, buybacks, partnership profit shares, or leave it as retained earnings. Changes in tax policy, corporate law, or business structures can significantly alter the mix of reported income without indicating any underlying change in entrepreneurial behaviour. Looking only at the labels on tax returns can therefore be misleading.

4. Corporate return or earnings analysis specially to say reduction in industrial sales could be due to housing businesses in subsidiaries and upstreaming income as dividend. Also, overseas expansion through acquisitions or even local acquisition does not show up as sales in Standalone financials including P&L. They show up as treasury income or do not show up as sales at all.

5. Tax return data is at a very high level to do this kind of analysis and arrive at these conclusions. The disclosures of income and heads chosen is a very legal exercise only for the purposes of taxation. Nothing more. It need not be commercial or economic. As an Independent Director... all my directorship fees is included in "other sources" (by law). Other sources is Rentier. But my labour in acting as a director is not!!!

The article confuses the tax classification of income with its economic character. The data may be interesting and is not incorrect, but this is not the strong evidence needed to draw the conclusion that Indian entrepreneurs are increasingly becoming "rentier".

Anecdotally, I can agree with the conclusion also. But I cannot agree that this data proves it.


Roshan Kishore: 1. India’s rich, incl corporates, are increasingly becoming rentiers than entrepreneurs
2. Both tax & corporate earnings data show the rise of rentier incomes rel to profits
3. Its perfectly legal but diverts “animal spirits” towards speculation from growth driving investment

items.title: 🧵 New Data Byte: The number of homicide victims in India has fallen, but only for men, by Ameya Bokil The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime ...
items.description_html:
🧵 New Data Byte: The number of homicide victims in India has fallen, but only for men, by Ameya Bokil

The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) defines intentional homicide as "unlawful death inflicted upon a person with the intent to cause death or serious injury". In India, the UNODC includes the crimes of murder, culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and dowry death based on the reports of India's National Crime Records Bureau, as intentional homicide. The total number of victims of intentional homicide has reduced since 1990 according to this data.

In 1992, the number of intentional homicides in India reached its peak with nearly 50,000 victims, and has since been on the decline. By 2022, this number had come down to 40,000.

Since 1999, when gender disaggregated numbers were first made available, the number of male victims of intentional homicide has reduced by nearly a third, from 33,000 to 24,000 in 2023.

On the other hand, the number of women victims has not declined in a similar way. From 14,000 deaths in 1999, the number of female victims of intentional homicide climbed to 19,000 in 2011 before declining to 16,000 in 2022, a number still substantially higher than it was in 1999. Of the 16,000 deaths, 6500 deaths are dowry deaths.

This suggests that the decline in homicides and homicide rates in India has largely been driven by a decline in homicide rates among male victims only, and not for female victims.

#Murder #Homicide #Law #India #DataForIndia

items.description_html:
RT The Indian Express
The Supreme Court on Thursday questioned how the Bihar government could retain Panchayati Raj Minister Deepak Prakash despite his remaining unelected beyond the six-month limit prescribed under Article 164(4) of the Constitution.

Hearing a plea challenging Prakash's reappointment, a Bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asked the state to explain its position, observing, "How are you retaining a minister beyond 6 months when he is not elected?"

The petitioner has argued that Prakash, first sworn in as minister on November 20, 2025, and reappointed on May 7, 2026, after a new council of ministers was formed, could not continue in office without getting elected within the constitutional timeframe. The plea contends that the reappointment circumvents constitutional safeguards and undermines representative democracy.

The Supreme Court said it would not grant the state any more time to file its response and listed the matter for hearing on August 4.

NEW: What's the status of US-China decoupling? How have Trump's tariffs in 2018-19 plus 2025 affected supply chains & US imports? @ChadBown explores.
💡Despite the US tariff actions, US real goods imports from the world in 2025 increased by 4% over 2024 levels.
📈By the end of 2025, US imports from the world remained above the pre-Trump 1.0 trade war linear trend.
📉US imports from China fell by 28% in 2025.
📈US imports from the rest of the world increased by 9%.
🇨🇳China’s share of US imports fell from nearly 22% in the 12 months before June 2018 to only 9% in 2025.
Other economies significantly increased their shares of US imports...
🇹🇼Taiwan by 4.1 percentage points
🇻🇳Vietnam by 3.7 points
🇲🇽Mexico by 2.3 points

💡The US imports from China hit hardest in Trump’s second trade war were those that were omitted from his first.
📈At the beginning of 2025, imports of products that had been omitted from tariffs during the first Trump administration were greater than they were before the Trump 1.0 trade war.
🗓️A 20% tariff on those goods by March 2025 led to a sharp decline in China's exports to the US.
📉In contrast, US imports of Chinese goods that had been hit with 25% tariffs in 2018–19 had already dropped by roughly 40% by the January 2025 inauguration.

items.description_html:
RT Mark Zandi
The economy is soft and vulnerable. This is the clear message in today’s GDP, income, and spending data. Abstracting from the vagaries of the data, real GDP growth is at best 2%, driven largely by AI-related investment and wealth effects that support consumer spending among the well-to-do. But housing, government, and international trade are more or less headwinds to growth. And given that real disposable income is flat and personal savings are about as low as they ever get, spending by middle- and lower-income households is under significant pressure. The longer the Iran war drags on, and the higher energy prices and interest rates go, the more likely these consumers are to pull back – and take the rest of the economy with them.

items.title: RT ANI: #WATCH | Mumbai, Maharashtra: On whether high US yields will offset the positive impact of index inclusion on Indian sovereign bond yields, Ca...
items.description_html:
RT ANI
#WATCH | Mumbai, Maharashtra: On whether high US yields will offset the positive impact of index inclusion on Indian sovereign bond yields, CareEdge Ratings Chief Economist Rajani Sinha says, “Rising US yields are a concern. It would result in US Treasuries looking more attractive compared to emerging markets. I don't see that as a big threat because there are chances of good inflows coming into the capital market because of the recent announcements. In fact, the data that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor spoke about regarding Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR) deposits—we are already looking at some $28–30 billion that has already come through FCNR. And then, as I mentioned, through Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) also, we have seen an improvement. On top of that, even if you look at Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) flows, the net FDI flows, the data that we have for the year so far, we have already got some $6 billion of net FDI flows. As against the whole of last year, when we had around $6 billion of net FDI flows, this year, in the first two months, we have already got more than $6 billion. So even on the FDI front, while gross FDI flows have been recording heavy growth, we expect the net FDI flows to also improve in the current fiscal year…”

items.title: RT ANI: #WATCH | Mumbai, Maharashtra: Speaking on how much Fed pauses and Bank of Japan moves restrict the RBI's headroom to cut rates in India, CareE...
items.description_html:
RT ANI
#WATCH | Mumbai, Maharashtra: Speaking on how much Fed pauses and Bank of Japan moves restrict the RBI's headroom to cut rates in India, CareEdge Ratings Chief Economist Rajani Sinha says, “Given the very fluid macroeconomic environment, we expect the RBI to maintain a status quo in the upcoming meeting. Going forward, the RBI is going to see how the growth and inflation data pans out, and based on that, there could be rate action in the subsequent meetings later in the year. We feel that there are chances of one or two rate hikes later during the year if inflation risks aggravate and if the RBI feels that inflation is becoming broad-based...”

On whether a stronger yen and a high-rate US dollar could spike rupee volatility and slow down FPI inflows, she adds, “Definitely, these concerns exist with the rising US yields and rates going up in Japan. There are concerns around flows to emerging markets, including India. But I would say that right now, there are also favorable factors for India, especially after the RBI announcements for capital flows and the government announcement, which are going to induce more inflows through FIIs. We have already seen FII debt flows of around $8 billion or so in the last two months...”

items.title: Rough move on the KOSPI, which went from 3000 to nearly 10,000 and is now at 5500. If you play momentum, you have to get out when the momentum's lost....
items.description_html:
Rough move on the KOSPI, which went from 3000 to nearly 10,000 and is now at 5500. If you play momentum, you have to get out when the momentum's lost. You will still make out very decently, if you don't go bonkers at the top.

The issue was with individuals in Korea taking leverage and participating when the markets were riding high. 3x levered single stock ETFs has to be the most clinically insane thing to do, just pure gambling. And then people borrowed money to buy these ETFs!

Indian regulators don't allow it, but then there is hidden leverage too - MTF (Margin Trade Funding) is growing. However India hasn't seen a major momentum move in stocks that will create a systemic issue yet.

The big boys in the memory world like SK Hynix, Samsung etc are falling not because their results aren't good - the results are brilliant. Yet, when prices fall through good earnings, you can almost tell that the momentum rise is done. (I've tweeted on this phenomenon earlier too)

The next complexity isn't the Hynix, or Samsung, or such, these are going to be cash rich. But the problem is in debt - the leverage taken by the players that hit these stocks is already getting hit. The leverage taken by AI players will be a big hit if there is actual slowdown in AI scale because competitors can bring far lower prices. The game is on.

•Members are ready for a hike: In the first split vote of the Warsh era, three FOMC members would prefer to raise rates in the face of elevated inflation.
•Warsh is trademarking his communication style: The new chair is opposed to forward guidance, preferring that markets and businesses react to real-time financial information.
•FOMC is letting markets take the lead: Warsh wants markets to react to economic shocks and news events in real time, rather than relying on Fed projections.

items.title: There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils ...
items.description_html:
There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils (mainly from Malaysia and Indonesia). The largest agri-economy has yet to secure its kitchen oils.

Both Indonesia and Malaysia are now levying export curbs and increasing domestic palm oil blending mandates for domestic energy production. Indonesia is already transitioning from B30 to mandatory B40 and planned B50 biodiesel blending, reducing global export availability. Malaysia is similarly expanding domestic palm oil blending mandates.

Bottomline: There is a massive shift amongst countries towards reducing crude oil imports and blending is the way forward. Ethanol in India, Crude Palm oil (CPO) for them.

Indonesia’s palm oil curbs could open the door for India to step up. What was earlier just an agri-policy (National Mission on Edible Oils) will soon be National priority. And unlike Energy security which is more challenging, this is an easier to solve problem. The acceleration is visible. Telangana and AP have championed the India Palm Oil mission, many more states are coming up now.

Which company fills the void? That's for investors to figure out. A good opportunity in the making.

Read:
https://www.fortuneindia.com/opinion/indonesias-palm-oil-curbs-could-open-the-door-for-india-to-step-up/150389

The AI memory crash comes on the back of last quarter record profits.

Samsung chip division's single-year profits beat its past 40 years total profit. Last quarter > Last 2 years. Stock has halved in a month.

Micron grew profits by 1400%, stock down 40-45%. Projections talk of record numbers for next 2 years as well. TTM PE hardly 4-5x.

So, why the panic and correction?

1. One obvious reason is profit booking, with record leverage in system amplifying the fall. What unfolded the sell-off was fear - China's Open source model and DRAM buildup fears, bond market pressure etc.

2. The other is valuation mistake. Is trailing P/E the right metric for extraordinary earnings cycle? The risks are in future, not in trail. The lesser variables you have that can impact earnings visibility the better. Here, there are more than what an analyst can predict with confidence.

Is this a buying opportunity? Is there more correction left? I don't know. But I know that basing investment decision solely on the fall from peak is often a mistake.

#FearandGreed

items.title: 🧵 India is warming, but not evenly. Geography, elevation, land-use patterns, urbanisation and regional climatic conditions all shape how warming is...
items.description_html:
🧵 India is warming, but not evenly. Geography, elevation, land-use patterns, urbanisation and regional climatic conditions all shape how warming is experienced locally, leading to considerable variation across states.

Temperature anomalies, defined as deviations from a historical baseline, provide a clearer picture of how warming has evolved over time and across regions. Meaningful temperature anomalies depend on a clearly defined and standardised baseline. The current official baseline used by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) is the average for the period from 1991-2020.

To examine whether recent years are warmer than in the past, we look at two periods - the decade from 1970-1980 and the decade from 2015-2025 - and compare both with the IMD’s baseline temperatures.

We find that most states in India recorded negative anomalies relative to the 1991–2020 baseline, averaging around −0.3°C, during the 1970s. This means that this decade was colder than the current baseline, across most of the country.

Conversely, the period between 2015 and 2025 is dominated by widespread positive anomalies (averaging around +0.32°C nationally), with temperatures across most states consistently exceeding the baseline.

The strongest warming is concentrated across northern and northeastern India. Parts of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh record mean temperature anomalies of +0.5°C to +0.8°C above the 1991–2020 baseline.

Mountainous and ecologically sensitive regions experience particularly pronounced temperature increases.

#Climate #Temperature #Heat #India #DataForIndia

items.title: RT James E. Thorne: Memory Liquidation The AI memory market is not the telecom boom, and it is not the housing bubble. What we are seeing now is a lev...
items.description_html:
RT James E. Thorne
Memory Liquidation

The AI memory market is not the telecom boom, and it is not the housing bubble.

What we are seeing now is a leverage event: too much leverage, too much crowding, and too much exposure piled into the same trade, all of which now need to be unwound. That matters because a real supply crunch in memory has been amplified by positioning, acute shortages and sharply higher prices tied to AI infrastructure demand are real.

Yes the easy money in the AI trade has been made!

Let’s be explicit about what that means. Parabolic charts are not proof of durable fundamentals; they are often evidence of momentum, leverage, and borrowed conviction feeding on themselves. When a trade gets this crowded, price stops reflecting only supply and demand and starts reflecting how much fast money is trapped in the move.

The underlying AI demand story is still real, and the fundamental supply-demand imbalance still exists. AI demand has forced companies to fight for dwindling memory supplies, while chipmakers prioritized higher-margin data-center chips and memory prices spiked sharply over the past year.

But that does not mean every price swing is fundamental. Narrative follows price: when memory names surge, investors discover scarcity; when they break, they suddenly discover China risk or efficiency gains.

That is why the analogies to the 1990s telecom boom and the housing bubble are only partly useful. In those episodes, supply ran ahead of demand, too much fiber, too many houses. Here, demand has outrun supply, but the stock market layered excessive leverage on top of a real bottleneck.

As Graham observed, the market is a voting machine in the short term and a weighing machine in the long run. Right now, the vote is being driven by crowding, leverage, and forced selling.

Over time, the market will weigh the underlying AI demand and the still-tight supply picture on their merits. What is being liquidated is not the existence of demand. It is the leverage wrapped around the story.

Yes Parabolic charts that amplify crowded leverage one way bets should be avoided.

items.title: Where's FCNR(B) flow gone? @kantisoumya of @TheOfficialSBI says, they are in transit. So far (8 June-17 Jul), FCA up by $7.6 bn, while RBI deposit mob...
items.description_html:
Where's FCNR(B) flow gone? @kantisoumya of @TheOfficialSBI says, they are in transit.
So far (8 June-17 Jul), FCA up by $7.6 bn, while RBI deposit mobilization was $17.4 bn for FCNR(B) flows.
While RBI provides weekly change in FCA every Friday, every bank has a designated time during the week to swap these FCNR(B) deposits with RBI and get equivalent rupee resources. It's possible that FCNR(B) deposit numbers are being captured by RBI and becomes a part of FCA with a lag --with assumption that a large part of foreign exchange reserves is being recouped & adding to RBI's foreign exchange coffers.

Owing to this,  we expect for the next 15 days period (17 Jul-31 Jul) FCA inflows could touch $10-12 billion based on current trends.

It may also be noted that once the swap is done, there will be a corresponding liquidity injection (permanent and temporary) Thus, bank time deposits/ permanent monetary injection have increased by close to Rs 90,000 crores. Core liquidity / Temporary liquidity injection has already at ~Rs 5 lakh crore as of June 30 clearly indicating the impact of FCNR (B) inflows on liquidity.

HFCL will invest ₹215 crore to add capacity for 270,000 MMC and SNMT assemblies annually, with commissioning expected by September 2027

The capex represents a significant scale up while also shifting HFCL toward higher value connectivity products used inside AI and hyperscale data centers

2. Paras Defence has signed a MoU to set up advanced packaging OSAT facility at cost of 6200cr

Advanced packaging is one of the crucial bottlenecks in AI supply chain today. TSMC overflow is already benefiting companies like ASE Tech and Amkor

Paras wants to set up latest 2.5D/3D advanced packaging line

This is just a MoU at this stage and no funding and terms have been finalized

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/f78828b7-aedc-4412-a05f-33fafd4aaefb.pdf

3. SPEL Semiconductor plans major expansion and fundraising of up to ₹1,000 crore

SPEL has approved raising up to ₹500 crore through a Rights Issue/QIP and another ₹500 crore through overseas instruments including FDI or FCCBs

SPEL currently operates a semiconductor packaging and testing facility, it does not manufacture chips or wafers

It packages fabricated semiconductor dies into finished ICs and performs electrical and reliability testing

The funds will be used to modernize and expand its packaging, testing, automation and manufacturing infrastructure
The company also plans to apply for Central and State semiconductor incentives

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/90be6dd5-03e3-4a54-a9c0-a4ba4a1f8183.pdf

4. ICE Make enters into a joint venture with Japanese company Galilei to foray into HoReCa segment

Galilei will also invest 180cr in ICE Make via preference shares

Food Processing & Hospitality already contributes 15-20% of ICE Make’s revenue, while commercial freezers account for only 2%, leaving significant headroom to build a larger standardized HoReCa equipment business

Galilei brings established Japanese product technology and has around 30% share of Japan’s domestic commercial-refrigerator production

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/ICEMAKE_24072026125113_Outcome_of_Board_Meeting_final_2.pdf

5. Apollo Micro Systems receives Indian Navy approval to develop an Autonomous Underwater Surveillance System

Apollo Micro Systems has received a Make-II Prototype Sanction Order to develop SAVIOR-ASW, an unmanned semi-submersible vessel that can operate for extended periods and use acoustic sensors and AI/ML to detect and classify submarines and other underwater threats

The system would represent a first-of-its-kind indigenous capability in India and marks Apollo’s formal entry into autonomous maritime and underwater warfare systems

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/408de015-8d30-40a5-9dc6-87c5bc839242.pdf

6. Marine Electricals wins orders worth 376cr including a major order from Siemens for power distribution system that will be used in a Hyperscaler data center

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/MARINE_24072026133342_Signed_Regulation_30_Bagging_of_Order.pdf

7. Gabriel India enters ADAS and automotive electronics through JV with Korea-based HL Klemove

Gabriel India will acquire a 30% stake in HL Klemove India for around ₹935 crore, while the Korean parent will retain the remaining 70% stake

HL Klemove India manufactures ADAS radars, front cameras, autonomous-driving control units and software, along with automotive electronics such as braking and steering ECUs

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/6df251ee-57b5-48ab-836c-60d324de1105.pdf

8. Sona Comstar enters into a partnership with Japanese firm Densco Corporation

Sona Comstar and DENSO will establish two India based joint ventures to develop and manufacture traction motors, inverters, generators and eAxles for electric and hybrid vehicles

The first JV will focus on high voltage liquid cooled powertrain systems for passenger and commercial vehicles, with DENSO holding 51% and Sona Comstar holding 49%. This gives Sona access to DENSO’s inverter and hybrid technology and expands it beyond individual EV components into integrated powertrain systems.

In the second JV, Sona will transfer its existing two-wheeler and three-wheeler electric motor and controller business into a subsidiary. DENSO will acquire a 49% stake at an enterprise valuation of ₹1,750 crore, while Sona retains 51% and management control.

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/79c5700d-fea7-4065-9651-2c9e1365c5db.pdf

9. Indo Tech Transformers enters the 400 kV transformer segment for BESS projects

Indo Tech has received NTPC approval to manufacture 400 kV class transformers for BESS projects, expanding its product portfolio beyond the existing 220 kV range
It has also secured an initial order for two 90 MVA, 400 kV transformers through an EPC contractor

Large grid scale BESS projects require high voltage transformers to connect battery systems to 220 kV and 400 kV transmission networks
NTPC’s recent renewable and BESS tenders include 400/33 kV tie transformers and 400 kV pooling substations

The approval moves Indo Tech into a more technically demanding and higher-value transformer segment and positions it to participate in NTPC’s growing BESS and renewable power evacuation pipeline

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/b7377360-48aa-48ed-a80b-86a90e9b668e.pdf

10. Azad Engineering delivers India’s first indigenous 350 kg thrust class expendable turbojet engine

Azad has manufactured and assembled a 350 kg thrust class turbojet engine designed by DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment, and delivered the first unit to DRDO

This is not a fighter aircraft engine, it is built for a one time use defence platform, such as a missile or unmanned system, rather than a reusable aircraft

The development is significant because Azad is moving beyond manufacturing individual aerospace components to the complete assembly of an indigenous jet engine, establishing system level manufacturing capabilities in a technology mastered by only a few countries

items.title: Measuring whether a household owns physical assets such as a TV, refrigerator, or washing machine often helps us understand its economic situation. Th...
items.description_html:
Measuring whether a household owns physical assets such as a TV, refrigerator, or washing machine often helps us understand its economic situation.

The latest data on household asset ownership comes from the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) conducted by India’s National Statistics Office in 2024. The survey asks a representative sample of households if they possess any among a list of household assets. 

As of 2024, televisions are the most widely owned of these assets in India. About two-thirds of Indian households own a television. Refrigerators are also now common, with nearly half of all households owning one. Washing machines are the least commonly owned of the three assets. Only about one in five households owned a washing machine in 2024.

The ownership of these household assets has grown steadily in India.

In the early 1990s, just 10% of Indian households owned a television. TV ownership grew rapidly from the 1990s onwards, but the pace of growth has fallen in recent years, suggesting that household ownership of televisions is nearing saturation. The ownership of refrigerators, ACs/coolers and washing machines, on the other hand, began to accelerate from the early 2010s.

items.title: New Data Byte: More than a quarter of rural households have no separate kitchen, by @nileena_suresh There is no separate kitchen space to cook food in...
items.description_html:
New Data Byte: More than a quarter of rural households have no separate kitchen, by @nileena_suresh

There is no separate kitchen space to cook food in more than one in four rural households in India. Even in urban areas, nearly one in five households where cooking takes place indoors do not have a separate kitchen. 

The National Family Health Survey, conducted in 2019-21, asked household heads whether cooking is usually done inside the house, in a separate building, or outdoors. If cooking was done inside the house, the survey further asked whether there is a separate room used as a kitchen. The responses reveal that a large share of Indian households lack a dedicated cooking space.

A majority of urban households cook their food in a separate kitchen. In rural areas, on the other hand, fewer than half of households use a separate kitchen within the house.

These arrangements have major long-term health implications. Cooking without a separate kitchen means that smoke from stoves or chullahs can easily spread through the living space, reducing the indoor air quality and exposing all household members to harmful pollutants. Inhaling this for a prolonged period of time increases risk of respiratory diseases including lung cancer.
In most Indian households, this responsibility falls primarily on women, making them particularly vulnerable to the health risks associated with household air pollution. This is particularly the case in rural areas where fewer than half of households use clean cooking fuels such as LPG.
 
#Cooking #Household #LivingConditions #India #DataForIndia

items.title: The size and make-up of a country’s prison population often reflects its approach to crime and punishment, the state of its criminal justice system, ...
items.description_html:
The size and make-up of a country’s prison population often reflects its approach to crime and punishment, the state of its criminal justice system, and broader socio-economic conditions.

India had over 530,000 incarcerated people at the end of 2023, the fourth-highest prison population in the world. Data on India’s prisons and prison population comes from the National Crime Records Bureau’s (NCRB) Annual Prison Statistics report.

Prison inmates in India are classified into four categories. Convicts are people who have been found guilty of a crime and sentenced to imprisonment. Undertrials are those whose trials are still ongoing and who have not yet been found guilty. Detenues are people detained to prevent them from committing a crime. The fourth category, others, includes inmates who do not fall into the first three groups.

The vast majority of prison inmates in India have not been convicted of any crime. Three out of four inmates are undertrials, with convicts making up most of the rest. Offences such as murder, attempt to murder, rape and those under drug laws are the ones that send most people to prisons, whether as convicts or undertrials.

items.title: India’s economy can be categorised into three broad sectors – agriculture, industry and services. In the 1970s, agriculture was the single biggest c...
items.description_html:
India’s economy can be categorised into three broad sectors – agriculture, industry and services.

In the 1970s, agriculture was the single biggest contributor among the three, accounting for about 40% of India’s Gross Value Added. Today, it contributes less than a fifth of economic output. This is in line with global trends - as countries get richer, the share of industry, or services, or both, in their economies tends to grow, and the dependency on agriculture falls.

The majority of the value added in the Indian economy now comes from the services sector, even as the sector employs less than a third of the workforce.

India's services boom was driven primarily by trade and hospitality from the 1970s to the 2000s. Trade and hotels (includes repair services and restaurants), and transport and communications (includes storage and broadcasting) have a 17% share in both the economic value added and in the workforce in services.

The services boom of the last few years has been led, to a large extent, by services other than these, including professional services. These include information technology, legal and accounting services among others.

Some sub sectors under “other services” in particular produce significant economic contribution but relatively few jobs. Real estate, for instance, has a 0.2% share in India's employment. But it contributes 7% to the gross value added in the economy. Financial services, which includes banking, insurance, and investment services, employ 1% of the workforce but contribute 6% to the economy.

#Employment #Agriculture #Economy #India #DataForIndia

items.description_html:
We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025.

But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea.

> First key factor we observed was the product mix change, where the company's intent was to gradually move from its ICE component business to Aero/Defence/Semicon (ADS) business.

> This product mix shift was visible from the fact that margins had been improving over the last 2 quarters, and growth was starting to pick up. That's how it came under our filters.

> Going a little deeper, we understood that the kind of things it was doing in the ADS business were quite moated. It had a single-source monopoly on Airbus A350/A320 thrust-reversal gimbals with zero defects over 12 years; hogging (machining from solid billet vs. forging) is a much harder-to-replicate capability for aerospace tolerances.

> Also, in its semiconductor business, it was working with Lam Research, where this year their business is expected to go from $10M to $30M .

> Also, as per our channel checks, they had orders/interest from Rolls-Royce for aero-engine feelers, the MMRFIC JV (navy fuses, radars), and a Tesla ESS order.

> All these things were a confirmation of our thesis that management has the capabilities, and that the product mix is changing for good.

> They have also given strong guidance of ₹8,000 Cr in revenue, with ADS at 20–25% of overall business and blended EBITDA margins moving above the 20% mark.

On top of this, we also visited their facility, where we got to understand the manufacturing complexity involved in the components they make for their ADS business, and their capabilities in precision engineering.

The framework was simple: through scanning, found a business where earnings were breaking out and margins were improving > went through their earnings calls and found the story of the product mix change > mapped out the value chain and tried to understand Sansera's moat in the new business they were focusing on > visited their facility to verify our thesis on the company.

items.title: New Data Byte: The choice of baseline affects how we see warming, by Juhi Chatterjee One of the best measures to understand warming is through tempera...
items.description_html:
New Data Byte: The choice of baseline affects how we see warming, by Juhi Chatterjee

One of the best measures to understand warming is through temperature anomalies. A temperature anomaly is the departure of the temperature for a particular year from a baseline. Positive anomalies indicate warmer than average conditions, while negative anomalies indicate cooler conditions when compared to the baseline.

This baseline or reference period is also referred to as the Long Period Average (LPA), and represents the average climatic conditions over a multi-decadal period of typically 30 years when measuring changes in temperature.

Temperatures today are typically measured against a reference period of 1991-2020, which is the baseline now in use by the India Meteorological Department, the official source of climatological data in India. However, looking at a range of baselines can provide important insights.

Using older baselines, such as 1951-1980, produces larger positive anomalies for present day temperatures with the anomaly estimated to be 0.98°C in 2024. More recent baselines, such as 1991-2020 produce smaller anomaly values for the same year with anomalies reducing to around 0.65°C. An intermediate baseline of 1981-2010 shows warming of a magnitude in between the two at approximately 0.78°C for 2024.

Updating baselines is important for climate monitoring because newer reference periods represent the current climatic conditions experienced by populations better. At the same time, older baselines highlight the cumulative scale of long-term warming. All baselines, however, show a warming trend.

items.title: Over the last century, life in India has become safer. A key reason for falling mortality in India has been the sharp reduction in risks to infants’ ...
items.description_html:
Over the last century, life in India has become safer. A key reason for falling mortality in India has been the sharp reduction in risks to infants’ lives.

Across the world, early childhood, especially infancy (the period before a child turns one), is a time of relatively higher risk compared to later in life. In the poorer regions of the world, infancy is a particularly dangerous time, when a combination of birth disadvantages as a result of maternal undernutrition and the high risk of contracting communicable diseases pose significant challenges.

India’s Infant Mortality Rate, or IMR – the number of deaths among children under one year of age for every 1,000 live births in a year – has fallen dramatically. It is one of the main indicators public health experts use to track child health.

Over the past 50 years, India's IMR has fallen from 134 deaths of children aged less than one for every 1000 live births in 1971, to 25 in 2023.

While infant mortality remains higher in rural than in urban areas, this gap has narrowed significantly in the last few decades. Although IMR is falling everywhere, poorer regions in India still have higher rates of infant mortality.

#Mortality #Deaths #Infant #Childhood #India #DataForIndia

items.title: An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works! You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either f...
items.description_html:
An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works!

You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either from a plant you own (merchant) or from a plant you build inside a customer's factory (on-site).

On-site is a 15-20 year annuity at thin margins. A merchant is a spot market where the same molecule earns very different money depending on the gas, the distance, and who else is selling nearby.

The whole game is capital, location, and the ability to squeeze extra high-margin gas (argon, liquid) out of a plant you've already built.

But let’s get into interesting details about that -

What does the industry actually sell?

Strip away the chemistry and this is an air-separation business. A cryogenic plant is an Air Separation Unit, or ASU that chills atmospheric air until its components liquefy at their different boiling points, and pipes off oxygen, nitrogen and argon at high purity. Everyone in the industry runs broadly the same technology, so purity differences are marginal (roughly plus-or-minus 5%). The molecule is a commodity. Almost everything interesting happens around the molecule in how it's contracted, delivered, and priced.

The demand base has historically been the heavy stuff: steel and metals, autos, pharma, healthcare, and a thin slice of chemicals and F&B. What's changing the growth story is the sunrise demand from solar and semiconductors, which pull large volumes of nitrogen and, in semis, demand purity that cheaper suppliers struggle to hit. That single shift is why every player in the country is pouring capital into new capacity at the same time.

The top four global MNCs Linde, INOX Air Products, Air Water India and Air Liquide India control roughly 80% of the market.

Below them sit regional, owner-driven players (Ellenbarrie, Vayu, Shree Ram Oxygas and similar) who have been around 10–15 years and whose space widened after COVID, when oxygen subsidies pulled local capital in.

Now let’s understand the 2 engines in this industry separately > on-site vs merchant

Everything downstream flows from one fork in the road: do you build the plant inside the customer's factory, or near a cluster of customers and truck the gas out? These are two genuinely different businesses with different economics, different customers, and different personalities.

> On-site - An anchor customer, usually a large steel plant, issues an RFQ saying, in effect, we need ~1,100–1,800 tonnes of gas a day flowing into our furnace. A supplier builds and operates an ASU on their premises under a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) contract running 15–20 years. The revenue is fixed and stable, so it's underwritten on a modest return — players will accept an operating margin of roughly 10–12%, sometimes pricing the whole thing to a ~10–15% IRR. It is deliberately boring money.

Why fight so hard for boring money? Because it's stable, long-dated and defensive with a 15–20 year foothold that also keeps a rival out of that customer. Contracts signed before roughly 2016–18 carried fatter margins and some still run (a few end around 2035), but the new-build market is now openly competitive on price.

> Merchant business - Here you own the plant, liquefy the output, and sell it as liquid, bulk or cylinders to whoever's within reach. Margins are structurally better but volatile: liquid/bulk runs a ~20–25% bottom line, while cylinder and specialty can reach ~40%. The catch is geography. Oxygen and nitrogen are cheap and heavy, so you can't economically truck them much beyond ~200–300 km before distribution cost (typically 10–12% of revenue) eats you alive. You plant an ASU, draw a 200–300 km radius, and fight for that circle.

The reason branded MNCs earn ~40–45% at the top while a strong regional player earns ~35% isn't a secret formula rather it's scale and mix. A Linde or INOX moves 4,000–5,000 TPD daily; a regional player moves 250–300 TPD. At a small scale, tender-driven medical demand keeps margins decent. But to scale from 300 TPD to 3,000–4,000 TPD you must chase the lower-margin sectors that make up the bulk of the market and that's exactly where pricing and margin pressure begin.

The value chain, end to end

Follow a molecule of oxygen from the atmosphere to the customer and you can see where value is captured and where it leaks.

Stage 1 - Build the plant (the capital gate)
This is a capital-intensive, power-intensive industry, and the entry cost is the first moat. A modest 200–250 TPD on-site plant needs at least INR 300–400 crore of initial capex. Core components are compressors, cold boxes that have to be imported; India makes none of them. Only fabrication and storage tanks (INOX, Cryolor, VRV) are domestic. Build time runs 16–24 months per ASU

Stage 2 - Choose your engineering partner (the quiet moat)
Who actually builds the plant is becoming the real differentiator. The MNCs carry in-house EPC muscle - Linde has Linde Engineering, INOX leans on Air Products' US technology which lets them build large, reliable ASUs and win the technically demanding jobs.
Regional players without that engineering wing increasingly tie up with Chinese OEMs on a sale-of-equipment basis: the Chinese firm builds and exits, and the local player does the O&M. It's cheaper (a 200 TPD plant runs ~INR 100–120 crore via a Chinese vendor vs ~INR 150–200 crore via an MNC), but blue-chip steelmakers (Tata, JSW, SAIL, AM/NS) often won't allow a Chinese machine where they're underwriting 15–20 years of reliability, power efficiency and capital backup, and they pay up for it.

The cost-vs-capability gap
> MNC plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 150–200 crore — technology, reliability, blue-chip acceptance.
> Chinese plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 100–120 crore — cost-optimised, favoured by smaller / secondary steel and rolling mills.
> No Indian regulation restricts Chinese ASUs, so the split is driven purely by which customer is buying.

Stage 3 - Extract the by-products (where margin hides)
A basic ASU makes oxygen and nitrogen. To pull argon you must bolt on a separate argon-recovery column and here's the quirk: that column costs roughly the same whether the plant is small or large, but a small 200 TPD ASU yields only ~5–6 TPD of argon while a big ASU yields 50–60 TPD. The capital-to-recovery maths favours scale heavily, yet argon's economics are so attractive that even smaller players are now installing the column anyway.

Stage 4 - Distribute (the tyranny of distance)
Oxygen and nitrogen are regional products which are heavy, cheap, and uneconomic beyond ~300 km. Argon is a national product valuable enough to ship across the country, though distribution then runs ~17–18% of revenue rather than 10–12%. This distinction quietly shapes the entire competitive map: oxygen/nitrogen competition is local and radius-bound, while argon competition is national and cyclical.

How to judge any player in this industry?
Pulling the mechanics together, a handful of questions separate a structurally strong operator from a fragile one regardless of the name on the door.

> Capacity trajectory: Can they actually double liquid capacity? You can't sell a molecule if you can't make expansion of 200 TPD takes 1.5 - 2 years, not six months.

> Mix quality: How much on-site annuity vs volatile merchant? How much argon and by-product upside are they extracting per plant?

> Engineering independence: In-house EPC, or dependent on Chinese OEMs who build and exit? This gates which customers they can win.

> Geographic competition: Are their plants in pockets with few rivals inside the 300 km radius, or in contested western/central India?

> Blue-chip acceptance: Can they clear the reliability/purity bar for Tata, JSW, AM/NS, and semiconductors or are they confined to secondary, cost-driven demand?

> Cycle timing: Are they adding capacity into the current glut, and can their balance sheet and geography absorb 2–3 years of merchant price erosion before demand catches up?

Dislaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.title: There are roughly 400 million men and 200 million women in India's workforce. But the nature of work is materially different between men and women in ...
items.description_html:
There are roughly 400 million men and 200 million women in India's workforce. But the nature of work is materially different between men and women in the workforce.

One of the principal differences between the way men and women work has to do with how they are paid.

In Indian labour statistics, workers may be classified as salaried workers if they have a regular job and are paid monthly. Casual workers work on someone else's farm or non-farm enterprise and receive daily or periodic wages. The self-employed get paid from the profits of an enterprise. Among the self-employed, one category of workers work on household enterprises but get paid no wages. They are termed as "unpaid helpers in household enterprises".

While some men do such unpaid work as well, women are twice as likely to be unpaid helpers. In comparison, less than half as many women are in salaried work.

This means that more than one in three working women, or 70 million women, are doing economically productive work, but for no wages. These are women who work in a household enterprise that is engaged in crop cultivation, milk and livestock production, retail sale of food, or small-scale manufacturing, but do not get paid for their work.

#Work #Women #Employment #LFPR #India #DataForIndia
